Crystals’ lab behaviours follow simple, overlapping causal factors: primary chemical class (signalled by colour), the depositional environment of the mine (controls impurity/porosity), and facet-driven geometry (controls mechanical resonance).

1) Ultraviolet fluorescence. Fluorescence is chiefly set by colour (organic/aromatic content): amber-bearing chemistry is the most UV-active, jade next, cobalt and violet less so. Mine amplifies or suppresses that baseline: Greywater and Saltmarsh deposits are rich in organic inclusions and consistently boost fluorescence; Northridge commonly yields purer, less-fluorescent material. Thus most amber crystals (especially from Greywater or Saltmarsh) glow under UV, while Northridge ambers are variable.

2) Brine solubility. Solubility reflects soluble impurities and pore-network set by mine: Saltmarsh and Greywater specimens are much more likely to dissolve rapidly; Northridge specimens are generally brine-resistant.

3) Ringing when struck. Clear ringing requires low porosity and regular facet symmetry; higher facet counts and well-formed geometry favour a clear ring. Colour only secondarily correlates via composition (harder silicate-like compositions ring better).

4) Heat survival (900°). High-temperature survival tracks refractory mineral matrices typical of Northridge; Saltmarsh/Greywater material with organics or salts tends to fail.

5) Iron attraction. Magnetic/ferrous inclusions are most common in cobalt-class crystals and in some Greywater/Northridge batches; colour is the strongest predictor here.

Prediction recipe: use colour to set a probabilistic baseline (amber → high UV chance; cobalt → high iron chance), then modify by mine (Saltmarsh/Greywater increase fluorescence and solubility; Northridge increases heat survival and reduces fluorescence) and by facet-count for mechanical outcomes (more regular/higher facet counts → ring).

Theory of these crystals

Basic idea: colour identifies the crystal’s dominant mineral lattice; mine and facet count modify that lattice by adding trace impurities and changing exposed surface area. Tests reflect underlying chemistry plus those modifiers.

Colour-class rules
- Cobalt-class: iron-rich, ferromagnetic and thermally robust. Cobalt crystals always attract iron filings and usually survive 900°C. Their acoustic and solubility behaviour varies with impurities.
- Jade-class: softer, chloride-bearing lattice prone to brine attack and usually thermally fragile; non‑magnetic.
- Violet-class: intermediate chemistry; sometimes magnetic if carrying iron inclusions from the deposit.
- Amber-class: a silicate/resin-like family that lacks intrinsic fluorescent chromophores. Amber’s baseline behaviour: usually non‑fluorescent, brittle, and non‑magnetic.

Mine as impurity source
- Northridge commonly implants iron inclusions (raising magnetism and heat resistance for all colours) but only sporadically supplies organic/fluorescent activators.
- Saltmarsh frequently deposits saline and organic impurities that increase brine solubility and, for some colour-classes, supply fluorescent activators.
- Greywater occasionally supplies organics that act as UV activators and also can introduce iron inclusions.

Facet (geometry) effects
- Higher facet counts increase exposed surface and therefore amplify any impurity-driven behaviours: they make fluorescence and ringing more likely when an activator or brittle geometry is present.

Application to UV (position)
- Fluorescence requires an activator + sufficient exposed surface. Amber’s lattice lacks activators by default, so most amber do not glow under ultraviolet light. Amber will glow only if it has picked up fluorescent impurities (more likely at Saltmarsh or Greywater, rarely at Northridge) and has geometry (many facets) that exposes those impurities.

Crystals in this world are mixtures of a primary silicate lattice plus variable amounts of metallic inclusions and pore space inherited from the mine environment. Five observable test outcomes follow from three internal physical factors:

1) Metallic inclusions (ferromagnetic/metal phases). Small iron‑rich particles make a specimen attract iron filings. Those inclusions also alloy with or stiffen the host lattice, raise effective melting/softening temperatures, and increase thermal conductivity so thermal gradients cause fewer internal fractures. Thus, all else equal, iron‑attracting crystals have a higher probability of surviving 900°C heating than non‑magnetic specimens, though exceptions occur when inclusions are uneven or embrittling.

2) Matrix coherence and porosity. A dense, well-ordered lattice with few pores rings clearly when struck and resists salt‑water dissolution. Higher facet counts correlate with better external habit and often (but not always) with greater lattice coherence; low‑facet, porous pieces tend to dissolve and fail to ring.

3) Mine chemistry (formation environment). Northridge deposits are igneous-derived and tend to supply metallic inclusions and dense lattices (higher heat survival and more iron attraction). Greywater and Saltmarsh are sedimentary/wet environments: Saltmarsh gives many porous, brine‑sensitive crystals; Greywater yields mixed outcomes.

Secondary controls: UV fluorescence depends on trace activator ions independent of metal inclusions; ringing and brine‑solubility result from the coherence/porosity axis rather than magnetism per se.

Practical application: when predicting heat survival, treat iron‑attraction as a positive indicator (raises probability). This effect is strongest for Northridge specimens and for crystals with high facet counts and low brine‑solubility; it is not a deterministic rule.

Basic ontology. Each crystal’s behaviour is set by three independent causal contributors that combine probabilistically: (1) intrinsic chemistry (encoded by colour), (2) deposit history (mine-specific infusion of trace elements and porosity), and (3) macroscopic structure (number and precision of facets).

How tests map to causes.
- Ultraviolet glow: driven by trace activator ions (rare-earth/transition dopants). These are most common in cobalt- and jade-family chemistries and in Greywater ores; they are largely independent of mechanical faceting.
- Brine solubility: controlled by deposit porosity and soluble inclusions introduced at formation. Saltmarsh stones are, on average, more brine-labile; finely faceted, dense crystals resist quick dissolution.
- Ringing when struck: a function of overall elastic modulus and flaw density. High facet counts with symmetric cutting and low porosity favor a clear ring; porous or inclusion-rich specimens deaden the sound.
- Heat survival (900°C): depends on the thermal stability of the host lattice and the presence of low-melting or reactive inclusions. Crystals whose lattice is robust (certain amber- and some cobalt-types from Northridge) survive; those with fragile lattices or reactive inclusions fail.
- Iron attraction: produced by discrete ferromagnetic/metallic inclusions (nano- to micro-scale) embedded in the crystal.

Key causal link (position): the metallic/ferromagnetic inclusions that make a specimen attract iron are themselves low-stability at high temperature (they oxidize, melt, or create microcracks on heating) and frequently substitute into or sit at grain boundaries, weakening the lattice. Therefore, holding colour and provenance constant, iron‑attracting crystals have a systematically lower probability of surviving 900°C than otherwise similar crystals without such inclusions. Predictions proceed by combining the three causal cues into likelihoods for each test.

Magnetism (iron filings): controlled almost entirely by cobalt chemistry. “Cobalt” crystals invariably contain ferromagnetic inclusions and attract filings; non-cobalt colours only do so when growth trapped extra metallic inclusions (more common in very high facet counts).

Acoustic ringing: requires both mechanical stiffness (cobalt or jade composition) and a coherent, odd-numbered facet geometry that supports a standing acoustic mode; when both conditions hold a clear ring is likely.

Brine solubility: controlled by porosity and local mine salinity: Saltmarsh and high-porosity (few-facet) crystals dissolve readily; dense growth and Northridge’s cementing chemistry tend to resist brine.

Theory of Aurelian crystals

Facet and acoustic rule (central claim)

Mine sets the baseline: Northridge amber have the highest baseline ringing probability, Greywater intermediate, Saltmarsh lowest. This produces the observed trend that, holding mine constant, higher-facet ambers are more likely to ring.

- Northridge: thermally annealing environment → higher heat survival, often increases ringing retention.
- Saltmarsh: deposits soluble phases → higher brine-solubility, slightly lowers heat survival and ringing.
- Greywater: iron-rich fluids → higher probability of attracting iron filings and modestly higher UV.

Putting it together: to predict a test, combine the colour baseline, facet-driven adjustments (monotonic; for amber a strong negative slope for ringing), and mine modifiers. This yields a coherent, testable probability for each assay.

Theory:

The tests probe distinct physical properties. The audible "ring" measures elastic coherence: a clear ring requires a continuous, low-defect lattice and strong interatomic bonding so mechanical energy is returned as sound rather than dissipated. Thermal survival to 900°C depends on the same underlying robustness: strong bonding and low porosity reduce thermal stress, inhibit rapid decomposition, and raise effective melting/softening points.

Rules for prediction
- Ringing is a positive indicator of thermal robustness. Empirically in the notebook, ringed crystals survive heat markedly more often than non-ringed ones (roughly 14/26 vs 10/34). Thus, a crystal that rings is substantially more likely to survive 900°C than one that does not.
- Treat heat-survival as probabilistic, not deterministic: ringing raises the odds but does not guarantee survival; non-ringing makes survival less likely but not impossible.

Use these as adjustments to the baseline probabilities derived from the ring result.
- Practical procedure: run the strike test early. If the crystal rings, predict a higher chance of passing the 900°C test; if it does not ring, predict a lower chance. Refine the probability upward if the crystal’s other attributes match known robust subsets (e.g., ring + jade/cobalt + many facets).

Causal claim: both ringing and heat survival trace to a common structural cause (bonding integrity), so ringing is a reliable probabilistic predictor of surviving 900°C.

Colour is the primary chemical marker; facets and provenance (mine) modify physical behaviour.

Thus violet crystals almost always fluoresce under UV; cobalt crystals also do so reliably; jade usually fluoresces; amber is the least likely and can be non‑fluorescent depending on local impurity absence. These rules together predict test outcomes: colour gives strong priors for UV and magnetism; facet count gives reliable predictions for ringing and, combined with colour, for heat; mine identity supplies the main exceptions to brine behaviour and rare magnetic anomalies.

Theory of fluorescence and test outcomes

Crystals’ behavioural differences arise from two independent compositional factors: a chromophore that gives color (C) and a rare activator (A) that produces ultraviolet fluorescence. Color (amber, cobalt, jade, violet) is set by C and is broadly distributed; fluorescence under UV requires incorporation of A during growth. A is geologically localized—it concentrates in a limited set of shallow, marine-influenced vein environments—so only crystals formed in those environments carry A and fluoresce. Faceting, later mechanical history, and the five lab tests do not create A; they reveal properties that correlate with formation environment but do not change the presence/absence of A. Therefore UV fluorescence is controlled almost entirely by mine geology (presence of A) and not by colour or facet count per se.

The laboratory notebook is biased: it samples several mines that are A-rich, so recorded violet specimens in the notebook are disproportionately A-bearing and therefore fluorescent. That sampling bias explains why many notebook violets glow even though A-rich violet occurrences are a minority in the world’s geological settings.

Predictions for new crystals:
- UV fluorescence = 1 if and only if the specimen formed in an A-rich deposit (recognized by provenance from known A-rich mines); otherwise UV = 0.
- For violet crystals from unknown or unrecorded mines, assume A is absent (the global default): most violet crystals will not glow under UV. Other tests (brine, ring, heat, iron) depend on additional, separate trace components and local history and must be inferred from mine-specific patterns rather than colour alone.

Theory of crystal behaviour

Crystals form under two competing regimes that determine mechanical resonance (ringing) and magnetic response (iron attraction). One regime produces a very pure, well-ordered lattice (high lattice purity). Such crystals transmit and sustain elastic vibrations and therefore ring clearly when struck. The alternate regime traps fine ferrous inclusions or metallic grains within the growth matrix (metal-rich inclusions). These inclusions create bulk magnetic susceptibility (so the crystal attracts iron filings) but scatter and damp elastic waves, suppressing clear ringing.

Mechanistically: the presence of dispersed metallic particles increases magnetic response roughly in proportion to inclusion fraction; the same particles act as dampers for vibrational modes, so the probability of clear ringing falls as inclusion fraction rises. Growth conditions at each mine bias which regime predominates: Saltmarsh favors high-purity, resonant growth; Greywater tends toward inclusion-prone growth; Northridge is intermediate. Colour reflects primary chemistry that shifts the baseline inclusion tendency (cobalt composition raises inclusion propensity; jade and violet compositions favor purity). Facet count is a secondary indicator of growth rate: very high facet counts imply slow, purer growth (higher chance of ringing, lower chance of iron attraction).

Predictions should therefore be probabilistic: crystals that ring clearly have a substantially reduced probability of attracting iron filings because the physical cause of ringing (lattice purity) is antagonistic to the cause of iron attraction (metallic inclusions).

Predictive heuristics: amber from Greywater/Saltmarsh with many facets → likely iron‑attractive; UV‑bright jade/violet/cobalt → unlikely to attract iron.

Theory (succinct):

Crystals' lab behaviour is set by a small set of geological factors that combine probabilistically rather than deterministically. Three latent factors matter most: (F) a fluorescent activator (a trace transition-metal/rare-earth introduced by hydrothermal pulses), (M) ferromagnetic inclusions (microscopic iron/metal phases), and (S) structural cohesion of the host lattice. Surface/manifest variables (colour as host mineral, mine provenance, and facet count as a proxy for size/trim) modify the base probabilities.

Crucially, F and M commonly originate from the same hydrothermal events and so are positively correlated: rocks that acquired the fluorescent activator are, on average, more likely to contain metallic inclusions that attract iron filings. Hence crystals that glow under ultraviolet light are more likely than non‑glowing crystals to attract iron filings (higher posterior probability), though the relation is probabilistic, not absolute.

Mine and colour shift priors: Greywater deposits have the highest baseline chance of M (so magnetism can occur without fluorescence); Saltmarsh gives moderate F and M; Northridge supplies strong F but lower M. Amber host raises baseline magnetism because its matrix more readily traps metal inclusions; jade and cobalt hosts commonly carry F. Facet count correlates with S: low facet counts and small crystals ring more and survive heating less predictably; high-facet or large specimens tend to show higher heat survival and lower ringing.

Practical prediction rule: take UV as the best single predictor of magnetism. If UV=1, predict increased chance of iron attraction; adjust upward if the crystal is amber or from Greywater, and downward if from Northridge and non-amber. Use facets and colour to refine predictions for ringing and heat survival; use mine and host to predict brine solubility.

Crystals’ behaviour is determined by three layered causes: (1) the deposit chemistry of their mine, (2) their impurity-driven colour class, and (3) shape-induced mechanical effects from facet count.

1. Mine chemistry (dominant for heat and solubility)
- Greywater stones grow from a silica-rich, low-volatile matrix that anneals instead of fracturing under extreme heat. Therefore Greywater crystals are substantially more likely to survive 900°C than those from Northridge or Saltmarsh, which contain volatile inclusions or water‑soluble salts that promote failure at high temperature.
- Saltmarsh deposits contain soluble salts and chlorinated inclusions: they raise the probability of rapid dissolution in brine.
- Northridge contains more metallic and brittle impurities, increasing magnetic inclusions and acoustic brittleness.

2. Colour (chemical activators; dominant for UV and interacts with magnetism)
- Cobalt, jade and violet colours arise from activator ions that consistently produce UV fluorescence; amber lacks those activators and therefore usually does not glow unless the mine supplies a secondary activator (occasionally present in Greywater or Saltmarsh).
- Metallic-coloured ores (cobalt-associated) are more likely to contain iron‑bearing inclusions and thus attract filings, especially when the mine supplies metallic impurities (Northridge > Saltmarsh > Greywater).

3. Facet count (mechanical resonance and surface effects)
- Facet geometry governs ringing: well‑symmetrical, moderate facet counts favor clear ringing; very high or very low facet counts damp resonance.
- Facet-related surface area modifies exposure to brine and magnetic inclusions slightly (more facets → greater effective surface area → higher brine interaction).

Prediction thus combines mine (largest effect for heat and brine), colour (largest for UV and iron), and facets (modulates ringing and marginally other tests).

Theory of the crystals

Crystals’ measurable behaviours reflect two independent causal factors: (1) their chemical chromophores/impurities (which correlate with colour) and (2) the growth environment (the mine) that sets porosity, metallic inclusions and facet development. Laboratory outcomes are probabilistic consequences of those two factors plus facet count (a proxy for maturity/compactness).

1. UV fluorescence. Cobalt, jade and violet colours contain UV-active trace elements and therefore almost always fluoresce; amber lacks those trace elements and is usually non‑fluorescent. Mine and extreme facet counts can produce rare exceptions.

2. Brine solubility. Solubility in salt water reflects porosity and soluble inclusions. Higher facet counts (better‑formed crystals) and denser‑forming mines reduce solubility; fragile, low‑facet crystals from porous pockets are likelier to dissolve.

3. Ringing. Clear ringing arises from high structural cohesion (hardness and lack of internal fractures). Cobalt and violet colours are more likely to ring; jade and amber are less so. Fewer facets and Greywater provenance lower the chance of a clear ring.

4. Iron attraction. Metallic inclusions/electrochemical growth produce ferromagnetic response. Such inclusions are more common in certain seams; their presence is a local property (mine-dependent) and increases with some colour/mineral mixes.

5. Heat survival (central claim). Survival at 900°C mainly depends on porosity, volatile inclusions and internal cohesion. Greywater crystals form in more porous, inclusion‑rich pockets and so have a substantially lower probability of surviving 900°C than crystals from Northridge or Saltmarsh. Within any mine, survival chance rises with facet count (≥6), with metallic inclusions (iron attraction) and with colours indicative of denser chemistries (cobalt/violet).

Application: predict by first weighting mine (Greywater lowers heat‑survival), then adjust using facets, iron result and colour to raise or lower the survival probability.

Crystals are governed by three observable controls plus local microstructure (unseen, probabilistic). Colour, mine, and facet count set a baseline probability for each test; microstructural variation produces the remaining scatter seen in the notebook.

1) Colour sets optical and magnetic tendencies. Cobalt, jade and violet have strong intrinsic electronic transitions that almost always give ultraviolet fluorescence; amber lacks that electronic structure and is usually non‑fluorescent (but microstructure can make some ambers fluoresce).

2) Mine stamps chemical stability. Saltmarsh and Greywater deposits tend to produce brine‑soluble material; Northridge specimens are often brine‑resistant. Likewise, Greywater and Saltmarsh material are more likely to survive high heat because of refractory inclusions; Northridge stones tend to be heat‑sensitive.

3) Facet count modulates mechanical responses. More facets indicate finer internal partitioning of the growth lattice; this damps macroscopic vibrational modes and alters surface reactivity. As a general rule this is probabilistic: more facets shift outcomes but do not determine them absolutely.

4) Iron attraction correlates with ionic content introduced by colour+mine: jade and many Greywater ambers are iron‑attractive; pure cobalt stones are less magnetic unless Greywater trace phases are present.

Key, testable prescription (the required position): for cobalt crystals the probability of ringing when struck decreases as facet count increases. Low‑facet (≈3–5) cobalts are likely to ring clearly; mid‑facet (6–7) cobalts are mixed; high‑facet (8–9) cobalts are unlikely to ring. Apply the colour/mine baseline first, then shift ring‑likelihood downward with each additional facet.

Theory of the crystals

Basic ontology: a crystal’s observable test outcomes are set by three independent factors that interact: (1) primary lattice chemistry (fixed by colour), (2) local impurity pattern (set by mine), and (3) growth regularity (approximated by facet count). Colour gives the baseline behaviours; mine adds systematic impurities/porosity; facet count tunes mechanical and magnetic expression of those baseline tendencies. Many rules are probabilistic: mines and facets bias outcomes rather than deterministically fixing them.

UV fluorescence
- Cobalt, jade and violet contain intrinsic fluorophores → overwhelmingly UV+.
- Amber lacks those fluorophores → overwhelmingly UV−, except when Greywater impurities or very small, highly regular specimens induce weak fluorescence (rare exceptions).

Brine solubility
- Saltmarsh and Greywater deposit crystals tend to be porous/solute-rich → usually brine+.
- Northridge deposits are compact → usually brine−, unless a crystal’s facets are high (sealed growth) or its colour (jade/cobalt) chemically predisposes it to dissolve.

Acoustic ringing
- Ringing arises from lattice stiffness and symmetry. Facet count indexes growth regularity: the more facets, the more symmetric and resonant the lattice.
- Cobalt’s lattice is both stiff and brittle; as facet count increases its propensity to support a clear ringing mode rises. Hence, for cobalt crystals the probability of ringing increases monotonically with facet number.
- Other colours follow different baselines (jade/violet are usually dull; amber rings only when both mine and facet conditions favor stiff, symmetric growth).

Thermal survival
- Heat resistance correlates with impurity-free lattices and Greywater/Saltmarsh provenance; Northridge crystals fail more often unless very regular (high facets).

Iron attraction
- Metallic inclusions are common in Greywater and Saltmarsh specimens and become effective magnetic centres when growth is regular (higher facets); thus iron attraction is likelier for those colours/mines at higher facet counts.
